lessons.title: Harvesting Techniques for Fingerlings
lessons.body: Harvesting fingerlings is stressful for the fish, so do it quickly and gently. The best time is early morning when temperatures are cool. Use a seine net with a soft, knotless mesh (1-2 mm) to avoid injuring the fish. In a typical earthen pond of 200 mÂ², two people can pull a 10 m net. Start at one end and pull slowly towards the other, keeping the net's bottom edge on the pond floor. When the net is close to the bank, lift it carefully and transfer fish into a holding tank or basin with pond water. For concrete tanks, you can lower the water level to about 20 cm, then use a scoop net to catch fingerlings. Never chase fish around the pond; it causes stress and mud. If you have many fish, harvest in batches. Sort immediately: any fish with signs of disease or injury should be culled. Work in the shade if possible. Have aeration ready in the holding tankâa small air pump or battery aerator works. If you harvest more than 5,000 fingerlings, use two holding tanks to avoid overcrowding. After harvest, return any broodstock or other fish to the pond quickly. Clean the net and dry it to prevent disease transfer. Record the number and weight of fish harvested. Remember, happy fish are healthy fish; rough handling can cause up to 30% mortality within 24 hours. So be gentle, be fast, and keep the fish in water at all times.

lessons.title: Grading by Size and Quality
lessons.body: Grading means separating fingerlings into groups of similar size. This is crucial because bigger fish eat more and can outcompete smaller ones, leading to stunted growth. Use a set of graded mesh boxes or a simple grading table with bars spaced at 5 mm, 8 mm, and 12 mm. For tilapia, grade at 2-3 week intervals. For catfish, grade every 10 days. Start by placing all fish in a tank with clean water. Then, using a scoop net, pour fish onto the top screen. Small fish fall through, larger ones stay. Work quickly but gently. You can also grade by hand: pick up fish one by one and place them in separate buckets based on size. This is slower but less stressful for small batches. Quality grading means removing any fish with deformities, cloudy eyes, or damaged fins. These are likely sick and should be culled. Also remove any predators or wild fish that may have entered the pond. After grading, count each group and record the numbers. Then move each group to its own tank or pond. Do not mix sizes again. If you are selling, graded fish fetch a better price because buyers want uniform sizes. In Africa, many farmers grade into three classes: small (under 2 g), medium (2-5 g), and large (over 5 g). Always use clean, dechlorinated water in the grading area. Add a little salt (1-2 g per litre) to reduce stress. Grading takes practice, but it pays off with faster growth and higher survival.

lessons.title: Counting and Biomass Estimation
lessons.body: You need to know how many fingerlings you have and their total weight (biomass) to plan feeding, transport, and sales. Counting every fish is slow and stressful, so use sampling. For small numbers (under 500), you can count by hand. For larger numbers, use the volume method: take a small container (e.g., a 100 ml cup), fill it with water, and count the fish in it. Do this 5 times and take the average. Then multiply by the total volume of the tank. For example, if 100 ml holds 20 fish, and your tank holds 100 litres (100,000 ml), then you have 20 x 1000 = 20,000 fish. For biomass, weigh a sample of 50 fish on a kitchen scale (0.1 g precision). Multiply the average weight by the total number. If 50 fish weigh 25 g, average is 0.5 g, and 20,000 fish weigh 10,000 g (10 kg). Always use a representative sample: mix the tank gently before scooping. For catfish, which are uneven, take samples from different parts of the tank. Record your counts in a notebook. This helps you track growth and feed conversion. If you are selling, buyers often ask for number and average size. Accurate counting prevents under- or over-feeding. Overfeeding wastes money and fouls water; underfeeding stunts growth. Weigh your fish every week to monitor. Use a digital scale if possible; they are cheap and accurate. A simple hanging scale with a bucket works too. Remember, 1 litre of water weighs 1 kg, so you can also weigh the container with fish and subtract the container weight. But the sampling method is faster.

lessons.title: Preparation for Transport: Conditioning and Fasting
lessons.body: Before transporting fingerlings, you must condition them. This means starving them for 24 to 48 hours. Fasting empties their gut, reducing waste in the transport water. Waste produces ammonia, which is toxic. For tilapia, fast for 24 hours; for catfish, 36-48 hours. During fasting, keep water clean and aerated. Do not feed. On the day of transport, do not feed. Also, lower the water temperature gradually by 2-3Â°C if possible. Cooler water holds more oxygen and slows metabolism. You can add ice in sealed bottles to the tank, but never directly. If you are moving fish in plastic bags, use clean, dechlorinated water. Add a small amount of salt (1 g per litre) to reduce stress. For every litre of water, you can pack 50-100 g of fingerlings for a 2-hour trip; for longer trips, reduce to 30-50 g per litre. Use oxygen gas to fill the bag: one part water, two parts oxygen. Seal the bag tightly with rubber bands. Place bags in insulated boxes or styrofoam coolers. For tank transport, use a tank with aeration and a lid. Fill only half full to allow oxygen exchange. Add a water conditioner like zeolite to absorb ammonia. If you are transporting in a vehicle, secure the tanks to prevent splashing. Avoid direct sunlight. Plan your route to minimize travel time. If you must stop, check fish every hour. If fish gasp at the surface, stop and add oxygen or change part of the water. Conditioning and fasting are not optional; they can mean the difference between 5% and 50% mortality. Always prepare the day before.

lessons.title: Transport Methods and Equipment
lessons.body: There are three main methods for transporting fingerlings: plastic bags, tanks, and baskets. For short distances (under 2 hours) and small numbers, plastic bags are best. Use 2-3 litre bags, fill one-third with water, add fish, then fill two-thirds with oxygen. Seal and place in a styrofoam box. You can fit 200-500 fingerlings per bag depending on size. For medium distances (2-6 hours), use 20-50 litre plastic jerrycans or drums. Fill half with water, add fish, and aerate with a battery-powered air pump. Keep the container covered to prevent splashing. For long distances (over 6 hours), use a transport tank (100-500 litres) with a built-in aeration system. You can also use a pickup truck with a tank and a small generator for aeration. Always use clean, dechlorinated water. Add 1 g of salt per litre. If you are using bags, do not stack more than three high. For tanks, secure them with ropes. In Africa, many farmers use baskets lined with plastic bags, but this is risky because oxygen depletes quickly. If using baskets, keep them shaded and change water every hour. Equipment you need: oxygen cylinder (for bags), battery aerator, thermometer, net, buckets, and a notebook. Test your equipment before loading. Never overload: a good rule is 1 kg of fish per 10 litres of water for a 6-hour trip. For every extra hour, reduce by 20%. If you are selling, transport early morning or late evening. Avoid midday heat. If you are moving fish between ponds on the same farm, you can use a wheelbarrow with a lined basin, but keep the distance short. Always have a backup plan: extra bags, oxygen, and water.

lessons.title: Acclimation and Release at Destination
lessons.body: When you arrive at your destination, do not dump the fish straight into the new pond. The water temperature and chemistry may be different, and sudden changes can kill fish. First, float the sealed bags in the pond for 15-20 minutes. This equalizes temperature. For tanks, slowly add pond water to the tank over 10-15 minutes until the tank is half pond water. Then, gently net the fish and release them into the pond. Do not pour the transport water into the pond; it may contain waste and diseases. If you are releasing into a tank, use a similar method. After release, monitor the fish for 30 minutes. Some may be stressed and swim erratically. That is normal. Do not feed for 24 hours after release. Let them settle. If you see many fish gasping at the surface, check water quality. Acclimation is especially important for catfish, which are sensitive to temperature changes. For tilapia, a difference of more than 3Â°C can cause shock. So always take your time. If you are releasing into a pond with predators, release at multiple points to avoid crowding. Also, release in the morning or evening when temperatures are cool. After release, record the number of fish, date, and pond. Check for dead fish the next day and remove them. If mortality is high, review your transport and acclimation steps. With proper acclimation, you can expect over 95% survival. Remember, the goal is to get healthy fingerlings growing quickly. A little patience at release saves a lot of loss.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: Early morning is cooler, reducing stress on the fish.

quiz.q: What type of net is recommended for harvesting fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: A soft, knotless mesh net minimizes injury to delicate fingerlings.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid chasing fish around the pond during harvest?
options: B) It causes stress and mud
quiz.explanation: Chasing causes stress and stirs up mud, which can harm fish.

quiz.q: What should you do with fish that have signs of disease during harvest?
options: D) Put them in a separate tank
quiz.explanation: Culling sick fish prevents disease spread to healthy stock.

quiz.q: How often should you grade tilapia fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: Grading every 2-3 weeks keeps sizes uniform and reduces competition.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of grading fingerlings?
options: A) To make them look pretty
B) To separate by size and quality
quiz.explanation: Grading separates fish by size and quality to prevent stunting and competition.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for grading by size?
quiz.explanation: Graded mesh boxes have bars of different spacing to sort fish by size.

quiz.q: What should you do with fish that have deformities?
options: B) Sell them at a high price
D) Release them into the wild
quiz.explanation: Deformed fish are often unhealthy and should be removed.

quiz.q: Why is adding salt during grading beneficial?
options: C) It makes fish grow faster
quiz.explanation: A little salt (1-2 g/L) helps reduce stress on fish during handling.

quiz.q: What is the volume method used for?
quiz.explanation: The volume method estimates fish numbers by counting a small sample and scaling up.

quiz.q: If 100 ml holds 20 fish and your tank holds 100 litres, how many fish do you have?
Why is accurate counting important?
options: B) To plan feeding and sales
quiz.explanation: Accurate counts help plan feeding, sales, and avoid overstocking.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh a sample of fish to monitor growth?
quiz.explanation: Weekly weighing helps track growth and adjust feeding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fasting time for tilapia before transport?
quiz.explanation: Fasting tilapia for 24 hours empties the gut and reduces waste.

quiz.q: Why is fasting important before transport?
options: B) It reduces waste and ammonia
quiz.explanation: Fasting reduces gut waste, which would otherwise produce toxic ammonia.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding oxygen to plastic bags during transport?
options: B) To increase oxygen for fish
quiz.explanation: Oxygen supports fish respiration during transport.

quiz.q: How much salt should be added per litre of transport water?
quiz.explanation: 1 g of salt per litre reduces stress without harming fish.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended density for a 6-hour transport trip?
options: A) 1 kg fish per 10 L water
B) 1 kg fish per 1 L water
C) 5 kg fish per 10 L water
D) 10 kg fish per 10 L water
quiz.explanation: 1 kg of fish per 10 litres of water is safe for a 6-hour trip.

quiz.q: Which transport method is best for long distances?
quiz.explanation: A transport tank with aeration provides oxygen and stable conditions for long trips.

quiz.q: What should you do if fish gasp at the surface during transport?
options: B) Add oxygen or change water
quiz.explanation: Gasping indicates low oxygen; add oxygen or change part of the water.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pouring transport water into the destination pond?
options: B) It may contain waste and diseases
quiz.explanation: Transport water may carry waste, ammonia, and pathogens.

quiz.q: How long should you float sealed bags in the pond before release?
quiz.explanation: 15-20 minutes allows temperature equalization.

quiz.q: What is acclimation?
options: B) Gradually adjusting fish to new water conditions
quiz.explanation: Acclimation is the process of slowly adjusting fish to new water temperature and chemistry.

quiz.q: When should you feed fish after release?
quiz.explanation: Waiting 24 hours allows fish to recover from stress before feeding.

quiz.q: What is a sign of stress in fish after release?
quiz.explanation: Gasping at the surface indicates stress or low oxygen.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record the number of fish released?
options: B) To track survival and growth
quiz.explanation: Records help monitor survival rates and plan future operations.

quiz.q: What is the expected survival rate with proper acclimation?
quiz.explanation: Proper acclimation can achieve over 95% survival.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a transport method for fingerlings?
quiz.explanation: Open buckets without aeration are not recommended due to oxygen depletion.

quiz.q: What should you do before loading fish for transport?
options: D) Cool them with ice directly
quiz.explanation: Testing equipment ensures everything works and prevents delays.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water temperature reduction before transport?
quiz.explanation: Cooling water by 2-3Â°C increases oxygen and slows metabolism.
